published by the II Party on 7.09.209. She did not prefer to put in an Application against such notification. She 
testified that she is not eligible to file application to the said post. Ex W-I] is the representation given by the I Party 
to the Chairman, LIC of India requesting to appoint her to the vacancy notified and if not, to keep vacant one post of 
Office Assistant till the instant case gets over. 


None of the above documents produced and relied upon by the I Party renders any proof to the core point 
of controversy as to the status of employment at the time of her engagement under the II Party. Indeed, had it been 
an engagement as Daily Wager, she does not get entitled for any of the benefits sought in the Petition. The II Party 
Management to buttress its contention that the I Party was simply disengaged as there existed no further requirement 
of her service and she has not been a temporary employee capable of claiming any of the benefits sought for, relied 
upon various judicial pronouncements of the Hon’ble Apex Court. At the threshold it has to be observed that the I 
Party failed in showing any Rule, Law or Regulation nor any administrative order on the basis of which she claims 
reinstatement and regularization with continuity of Service and other monetory benefits. In order to high light the 
said aspect the II Party has relied upon the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Subedar Singh and others vs. District 
Judge, Mirzapur and another 200I SCC 37. 


5. It is contextually significant to follow the dictum laid down by the Hon’ble Apex Court in State of 
Haryana vs. Jasmer Singh (996 (l) SCC 77) which reads : 


“The respondents, therefore in the present appeals who are employed on daily wages cannot be treated 
as on a par with persons in regular service of the State of Haryana holding similar posts. Daily-rated 
workers are not required to possess the qualifications prescribed for regular workers, nor do they have 
to fulfil the requirement relating to age at the time of recruitment. They are not selected in the manner 
in which regular employees are selected. In other words the requirements for selection are not as 
rigorous. There are also other provisions relating to regular service such as the liability of a member of 
the service to be transferred, and his being subject to the disciplinary jurisdiction of the authorities as 
prescribed, which the daily-rated workmen are not subjected to. They cannot, therefore, be equated 
with regular workmen for the purposes for their wages. Nor can they claim the minimum of the 
regular pay-scale of the regularly employed” 


Referring to the said legal position the Hon’ble Apex Court in State of Haryana and another vs. Tilak Raj and 
others (2003 (6) SCC 23) held that a scale of pay is attached to a definite post and in case of a daily wager, he 
holds no posts. The I Party neither in her pleadings nor in evidence has made out the particular works she 
performed under the II Party, much less any material is placed by her as to the nature of the duties for which she was 
engaged by the II Party. The contention of the II Party in its Statement of Objection that the engagement of the I 
Party was for meeting the office exigencies to attend some unspecified jobs on payment of daily wage for the work 
performed is thus well founded. 


6. In Mohammed Ashif and others vs. State of Bihar and others (200 (5) SCC 475), the Hon’ble Supreme 
Court held that the question of regularization of services of an Employee may arise only in situations where against 
an available clear vacancy an appointment is made on adhoc or on-daily wage basis by an authority competent to do 
so without any artificial break in service. The second situation in which the regularization could be granted is held 
to be where the initial entry of the employee against an available vacancy was found suffering from some flaws in 


5758 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA AUGUST 6, 2025/SHRAVANA 25, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


the procedure in making the appointment though the person appointing was competent to make such initial 
recruitment and had otherwise followed the procedure prescribed for such recruitment. It is equally held that “the 
all-important condition precedent for such regularization is that the initial entry of such employee must be made 
against the Sanctioned vacancy and by following the Rules and Regulations governing such entry”. 


7. Similarly the constitution bench of the Hon’ble Apex Court in State of Karnataka vs. Uma Devi (2006 (4) 
SCC ) held that “/fit is a contractual appointment, the appointment comes to an end at the end of the contract, if it 
were an engagement or appointment on daily wages or casual basis, the same would come to an end when it is 
discontinued. Similarly, a temporary employee could not claim to be made permanent on the expiry of his term of 
appointment. It has also to be clarified that merely because a temporary employee or a casual wage worker is 
continued for a time beyond the term of his appointment, he would not be entitled to be absorbed in regular service 
or made permanent, merely on the strength of such continuance, if the original appointment was not made by 
following a due process of selection as envisaged by the relevant rules. It is not open to the court to prevent regular 
recruitment at the instance of temporary employees whose period of employment has come to an end or of ad hoc 
employees who by the very nature of their appointment, do not acquire any right.’ Here in the instant case the I 
party is claiming permanency and seeks for regularization mainly on the so called “long duration of work” 
(emphasis supplied) and not on any other valid ground. The dictum quoted above defeats her claim as it is bereft of 
valid support and devoid of merit. 


8. Most of the rulings placed by the I party are not applicable to the facts of the case on hand. The Verdict of 
the Hon’ble High Court of Madras in V Muthukumarasamy and others vs. The Chairman, LIC, Zonal Office 
dated 2.0.2007 also does not get any application in view of the fact involved in that case as the Petitioners therein 
were sponsored by the Employment Exchange and have been appointed on temporary basis from shortlisted 
candidates. As already observed, the I Party herein was not sponsored by Employment Exchange nor her 
engagement was in a clear vacancy by undergoing the Regular Recruitment process. 


9. The I party further relied upon on the ruling of the Hon’ble High Court of Karnataka, Bengaluru in R V 
Mohan Reddy vs. The Chairman, Karnataka Grameena Bank in WP No. 944/2022 (L-RES) dated 
0.02.2025 awarding 60% of Backwages to the Employee from the date of his termination reckoning the two 
decades of service he had under the management as a Peon on daily wage. As against that, the principle laid down 
by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in a plethora of rulings aforementioned consistently hold that the Casual 
Employment terminates when the same is discontinued, and merely because a temporary or casual worker has been 
engaged beyond the period of his employment, he would not be entitled to be absorbed into regular service or made 
permanent, if the original appointment was not in terms of the process envisaged by the relevant rules. So the legal 
position settled at rest by the Hon’ble Supreme Court disentitles the I party to put forth any claim of reinstatement, 
regularization, continuity of service or back wages with consequential benefits. 


20. To sum up, the solitary materials viz., Ex W-l vouchers show only pay for a single month in the respective 
years and there is no valid material proving that her engagement was continuous in nature and she performed duties 
under the II Party continuously till the date of her disengagement so as to show that her tenure of service at a time 
was more than 240 days in a calendar year and her disengagement was in violation of the provisions of Section 25F 
of the ID Act. So on legal principle and on factual matrix the I Party failed to establish a case on merit justifying the 
relief sought for in the instant Industrial Dispute. Eventually her Claim Petition fails and the same is liable to be 
dismissed. With this view Points No. | to 3 are answered accordingly.

she was appointed as an Assistant by the 27 Party in a clear vacancy of Office Assistant w.e.f. 24.04.200 by 
obtaining an Application and she has attended the interview conducted by the II Party; she was also assured with 
regularization of her services for the services rendered by her and that she was doing the duties of regular staff; that 
she was not paid with minimum scales as applicable to the Assistants and took work for more than eight hours per 
day without paying her overtime wages; inspite of repeated requests to absorb her to the permanent post she was 
deprived with the benefits of the permanent employees; that she was not provided with Provident Fund, Bonus 
Benefits though other employees were extended with the same; that she was suddenly retrenched from the services 
of the II Party orally from |8.2.207 in the morning hours by the Branch Manager without notice, without payment 
of notice pay / retrenchment compensation though there were no allegations against her. She was retrenched from 
the services without prior intimation or paying her retrenchment compensation and without following due process of 
law and that the II Party has retrenched more than 20 workmen without filing approval application seeking

that due to the retrenchment she is facing irreparable hardship, agony and unable to run her family and that she does 
not know any other work than the Assistant job; that the II Party has employed fresh entrants in her place and the 
nature of work done by her is perennial in nature and taking the new entrants is illegal and malafide; that she raised 
an industrial dispute since no settlement was arrived she preferred to file the present petition requesting this Tribunal

7. The I Party WW | claimed herself as a temporary employee / Assistant in Class III Category in a clear

and she was interviewed by the officials of the LIC at the Branch Office. According to her she was appointed with 
an assurance of regularization of her service within a few years coupled with the benefits applicable to permanent 
Assistants. The above claim of the I Party is stoutly denied by the II Party on the precincts that the I Party was

8. Among the documents produced and proved by WW |, there is nothing indicting her to have been called 
for an interview for the post of Office Assistant. She did not produce copy of application said to have been

Those vouchers would never improve her case, much less it substantiates her contention that she was appointed in a

uninterrupted service of the I Party under the II Party for Seven years as contended by her.

during the conciliation proceedings. As per Ex W-7 the Assistant Labour Commissioner(C) conducted Joint 
Discussion on 05.02.20I8 notifying further joint discussion to another date. Ex W-8 is also a similar application 
filed by the I Party before the Conciliation Officer calling for some more documents from the II party during the 
conciliation proceedings. Ex W-9 is the letter issued by the ALC(C) to LEO for collection of photocopies of 
documents from various branches. Ex W-l0 is the copy of notification to the post of Recruitment of Assistant 
published by the IT Party on !7.09.209. She did not prefer to put in an Application against such notification. She 
testified that she is not eligible to file application to the said post. Ex W-I] is the representation given by the I Party 
to the Chairman, LIC of India requesting to appoint her to the vacancy notified and if not, to keep vacant one post of 
Office Assistant till the instant case gets over. 


4. None of the above documents produced and relied upon by the I Party renders any proof to the core point 
of controversy as to the status of employment at the time of her engagement under the II Party. Indeed, had it been 
an engagement as Daily Wager, she does not get entitled for any of the benefits sought in the Petition. The II Party 
Management to buttress its contention that the I Party was simply disengaged as there existed no further requirement 
of her service and she has not been a temporary employee capable of claiming any of the benefits sought for, relied 
upon various judicial pronouncements of the Hon’ble Apex Court. At the threshold it has to be observed that the I 
Party failed in showing any Rule, Law or Regulation nor any administrative order on the basis of which she claims 
reinstatement and regularization with continuity of Service and other monetory benefits. In order to high light the 
said aspect the II Party has relied upon the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Subedar Singh and others vs. District 
Judge, Mirzapur and another 200I SCC 37. 


5. It is contextually significant to follow the dictum laid down by the Hon’ble Apex Court in State of 
Haryana vs. Jasmer Singh (996 (l) SCC 77) which reads : 


“The respondents, therefore in the present appeals who are employed on daily wages cannot be treated 
as on a par with persons in regular service of the State of Haryana holding similar posts. Daily-rated 
workers are not required to possess the qualifications prescribed for regular workers, nor do they have 
to fulfil the requirement relating to age at the time of recruitment. They are not selected in the manner 
in which regular employees are selected. In other words the requirements for selection are not as 
rigorous. There are also other provisions relating to regular service such as the liability of a member of 
the service to be transferred, and his being subject to the disciplinary jurisdiction of the authorities as 
prescribed, which the daily-rated workmen are not subjected to. They cannot, therefore, be equated 
with regular workmen for the purposes for their wages. Nor can they claim the minimum of the 
regular pay-scale of the regularly employed” 


Referring to the said legal position the Hon’ble Apex Court in State of Haryana and another vs. Tilak Raj and 
others (2003 (6) SCC 23) held that a scale of pay is attached to a definite post and in case of a daily wager, he 
holds no posts. The I Party neither in her pleadings nor in evidence has made out the particular works she 
performed under the II Party, much less any material is placed by her as to the nature of the duties for which she was 
engaged by the II Party. The contention of the I Party in its Statement of Objection that the engagement of the I 
Party was for meeting the office exigencies to attend some unspecified jobs on payment of daily wage for the work 
performed is thus well founded. 


6. In Mohammed Ashif and others vs. State of Bihar and others (200 (5) SCC 475), the Hon’ble Supreme 
Court held that the question of regularization of services of an Employee may arise only in situations where against 
an available clear vacancy an appointment is made on adhoc or on-daily wage basis by an authority competent to do 
so without any artificial break in service. The second situation in which the regularization could be granted is held 
to be where the initial entry of the employee against an available vacancy was found suffering from some flaws in 


5766 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA AUGUST 6, 2025/SHRAVANA 25, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


the procedure in making the appointment though the person appointing was competent to make such initial 
recruitment and had otherwise followed the procedure prescribed for such recruitment. It is equally held that “the 
all-important condition precedent for such regularization is that the initial entry of such employee must be made 
against the Sanctioned vacancy and by following the Rules and Regulations governing such entry”. 
7. Similarly the constitution bench of the Hon’ble Apex Court in State of Karnataka vs. Uma Devi (2006 (4) 
SCC ) held that “/f it is a contractual appointment, the appointment comes to an end at the end of the contract, if it 
were an engagement or appointment on daily wages or casual basis, the same would come to an end when it is 
discontinued. Similarly, a temporary employee could not claim to be made permanent on the expiry of his term of 
appointment. It has also to be clarified that merely because a temporary employee or a casual wage worker is 
continued for a time beyond the term of his appointment, he would not be entitled to be absorbed in regular service 
or made permanent, merely on the strength of such continuance, if the original appointment was not made by 
following a due process of selection as envisaged by the relevant rules. It is not open to the court to prevent regular 
recruitment at the instance of temporary employees whose period of employment has come to an end or of ad hoc 
employees who by the very nature of their appointment, do not acquire any right.’ Here in the instant case the I 
party is claiming permanency and seeks for regularization mainly on the so called “long duration of work” 
(emphasis supplied) and not on any other valid ground. The dictum quoted above defeats her claim as it is bereft of 
valid support and devoid of merit. 
8. Most of the rulings placed by the I party are not applicable to the facts of the case on hand. The Verdict of 
the Hon’ble High Court of Madras in V Muthukumarasamy and others vs. The Chairman, LIC, Zonal Office 
dated 2.0.2007 also does not get any application in view of the fact involved in that case as the Petitioners therein 
were sponsored by the Employment Exchange and have been appointed on temporary basis from shortlisted 
candidates. As already observed, the I Party herein was not sponsored by Employment Exchange nor her 
engagement was in a clear vacancy by undergoing the Regular Recruitment process. 
9. The I party further relied upon on the ruling of the Hon’ble High Court of Karnataka, Bengaluru in R V 
Mohan Reddy vs. The Chairman, Karnataka Grameena Bank in WP No. 944/2022 (L-RES) dated 
0.02.2025 awarding 60% of Backwages to the Employee from the date of his termination reckoning the two 
decades of service he had under the management as a Peon on daily wage. As against that, the principle laid down 
by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in a plethora of rulings aforementioned consistently hold that the Casual 
Employment terminates when the same is discontinued, and merely because a temporary or casual worker has been 
engaged beyond the period of his employment, he would not be entitled to be absorbed into regular service or made 
permanent, if the original appointment was not in terms of the process envisaged by the relevant rules. So the legal 
position settled at rest by the Hon’ble Supreme Court disentitles the I party to put forth any claim of reinstatement, 
regularization, continuity of service or back wages with consequential benefits. 
20. To sum up, the solitary materials viz., Ex W-l vouchers show only pay for a single month in the respective 
years and there is no valid material proving that her engagement was continuous in nature and she performed duties 
under the II Party continuously till the date of her disengagement so as to show that her tenure of service at a time 
was more than 240 days in a calendar year and her disengagement was in violation of the provisions of Section 25F 
of the ID Act. So on legal principle and on factual matrix the I Party failed to establish a case on merit justifying the 
relief sought for in the instant Industrial Dispute. Eventually her Claim Petition fails and the same is liable to be 
dismissed. With this view Points No. | to 3 are answered accordingly. 
2. POINT NO. 4: In view of the above discussion, the I party is held as not entitled for any relief.

The Claim Petition is Dismissed. No order as to cost.

4. None of the above documents produced and relied upon by the I Party renders any proof to the core point 
of controversy as to the status of employment at the time of her engagement under the II Party. Indeed, had it been 
an engagement as Daily Wager, she does not get entitled for any of the benefits sought in the Petition. The II Party 
Management to buttress its contention that the I Party was simply disengaged as there existed no further requirement 
of her service and she has not been a temporary employee capable of claiming any of the benefits sought for, relied 
upon various judicial pronouncements of the Hon’ble Apex Court. At the threshold it has to be observed that the I 
Party failed in showing any Rule, Law or Regulation nor any administrative order on the basis of which she claims 
reinstatement and regularization with continuity of Service and other monetory benefits. In order to high light the 
said aspect the II Party has relied upon the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Subedar Singh and others vs. District 
Judge, Mirzapur and another 200I SCC 37. 


5. It is contextually significant to follow the dictum laid down by the Hon’ble Apex Court in State of 
Haryana vs. Jasmer Singh (996 (Il) SCC 77) which reads : 


“The respondents, therefore in the present appeals who are employed on daily wages cannot be treated 
as on a par with persons in regular service of the State of Haryana holding similar posts. Daily-rated 
workers are not required to possess the qualifications prescribed for regular workers, nor do they have 
to fulfil the requirement relating to age at the time of recruitment. They are not selected in the manner 
in which regular employees are selected. In other words the requirements for selection are not as 
rigorous. There are also other provisions relating to regular service such as the liability of a member of 
the service to be transferred, and his being subject to the disciplinary jurisdiction of the authorities as 
prescribed, which the daily-rated workmen are not subjected to. They cannot, therefore, be equated 
with regular workmen for the purposes for their wages. Nor can they claim the minimum of the 
regular pay-scale of the regularly employed” 


Referring to the said legal position the Hon’ble Apex Court in State of Haryana and another vs. Tilak Raj and 
others (2003 (6) SCC 23) held that a scale of pay is attached to a definite post and in case of a daily wager, he 
holds no posts. The I Party neither in her pleadings nor in evidence has made out the particular works she 
performed under the II Party, much less any material is placed by her as to the nature of the duties for which she was 
engaged by the II Party. The contention of the II Party in its Statement of Objection that the engagement of the I 
Party was for meeting the office exigencies to attend some unspecified jobs on payment of daily wage for the work 
performed is thus well founded. 


6. In Mohammed Ashif and others vs. State of Bihar and others (200 (5) SCC 475), the Hon’ble Supreme 
Court held that the question of regularization of services of an Employee may arise only in situations where against 
an available clear vacancy an appointment is made on adhoc or on-daily wage basis by an authority competent to do 
so without any artificial break in service. The second situation in which the regularization could be granted is held 
to be where the initial entry of the employee against an available vacancy was found suffering from some flaws in 
the procedure in making the appointment though the person appointing was competent to make such initial 
recruitment and had otherwise followed the procedure prescribed for such recruitment. It is equally held that “the 
all-important condition precedent for such regularization is that the initial entry of such employee must be made 


5770 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA AUGUST 6, 2025/SHRAVANA 25, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


against the Sanctioned vacancy and by following the Rules and Regulations governing such entry”. 


7. Similarly the constitution bench of the Hon’ble Apex Court in State of Karnataka vs. Uma Devi (2006 (4) 
SCC ) held that “/fit is a contractual appointment, the appointment comes to an end at the end of the contract, if it 
were an engagement or appointment on daily wages or casual basis, the same would come to an end when it is 
discontinued. Similarly, a temporary employee could not claim to be made permanent on the expiry of his term of 
appointment. It has also to be clarified that merely because a temporary employee or a casual wage worker is 
continued for a time beyond the term of his appointment, he would not be entitled to be absorbed in regular service 
or made permanent, merely on the strength of such continuance, if the original appointment was not made by 
following a due process of selection as envisaged by the relevant rules. It is not open to the court to prevent regular 
recruitment at the instance of temporary employees whose period of employment has come to an end or of ad hoc 
employees who by the very nature of their appointment, do not acquire any right.’ Here in the instant case the I 
party is claiming permanency and seeks for regularization mainly on the so called “long duration of work” 
(emphasis supplied) and not on any other valid ground. The dictum quoted above defeats her claim as it is bereft of 
valid support and devoid of merit. 


8. Most of the rulings placed by the I party are not applicable to the facts of the case on hand. The Verdict of 
the Hon’ble High Court of Madras in V Muthukumarasamy and others vs. The Chairman, LIC, Zonal Office 
dated 2.0.2007 also does not get any application in view of the fact involved in that case as the Petitioners therein 
were sponsored by the Employment Exchange and have been appointed on temporary basis from shortlisted 
candidates. As already observed, the I Party herein was not sponsored by Employment Exchange nor her 
engagement was in a clear vacancy by undergoing the Regular Recruitment process. 


9. The I party further relied upon on the ruling of the Hon’ble High Court of Karnataka, Bengaluru in R V 
Mohan Reddy vs. The Chairman, Karnataka Grameena Bank in WP No. 944/2022 (L-RES) dated 
0.02.2025 awarding 60% of Backwages to the Employee from the date of his termination reckoning the two 
decades of service he had under the management as a Peon on daily wage. As against that, the principle laid down 
by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in a plethora of rulings aforementioned consistently hold that the Casual 
Employment terminates when the same is discontinued, and merely because a temporary or casual worker has been 
engaged beyond the period of his employment, he would not be entitled to be absorbed into regular service or made 
permanent, if the original appointment was not in terms of the process envisaged by the relevant rules. So the legal 
position settled at rest by the Hon’ble Supreme Court disentitles the I party to put forth any claim of reinstatement, 
regularization, continuity of service or back wages with consequential benefits. 


20. To sum up, the solitary materials viz., Ex W-l vouchers show only pay for a single month in the respective 
years and there is no valid material proving that her engagement was continuous in nature and she performed duties 
under the II Party continuously till the date of her disengagement so as to show that her tenure of service at a time 
was more than 240 days in a calendar year and her disengagement was in violation of the provisions of Section 25F 
of the ID Act. So on legal principle and on factual matrix the I Party failed to establish a case on merit justifying the 
relief sought for in the instant Industrial Dispute. Eventually her Claim Petition fails and the same is liable to be 
dismissed. With this view Points No. | to 3 are answered accordingly. 


2I. POINT NO. 4: In view of the above discussion, the I party is held as not entitled for any relief.

4. None of the above documents produced and relied upon by the I Party renders any proof to the core point 
of controversy as to the status of employment at the time of her engagement under the II Party. Indeed, had it been 
an engagement as Daily Wager, she does not get entitled for any of the benefits sought in the Petition. The II Party 
Management to buttress its contention that the I Party was simply disengaged as there existed no further requirement 
of her service and she has not been a temporary employee capable of claiming any of the benefits sought for, relied 
upon various judicial pronouncements of the Hon’ble Apex Court. At the threshold it has to be observed that the I 
Party failed in showing any Rule, Law or Regulation nor any administrative order on the basis of which she claims 
reinstatement and regularization with continuity of Service and other monetory benefits. In order to high light the 
said aspect the II Party has relied upon the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Subedar Singh and others vs. District 
Judge, Mirzapur and another 200I SCC 37. 


5. It is contextually significant to follow the dictum laid down by the Hon’ble Apex Court in State of 
Haryana vs. Jasmer Singh (996 (l) SCC 77) which reads : 


“The respondents, therefore in the present appeals who are employed on daily wages cannot be treated 
as on a par with persons in regular service of the State of Haryana holding similar posts. Daily-rated 
workers are not required to possess the qualifications prescribed for regular workers, nor do they have 
to fulfil the requirement relating to age at the time of recruitment. They are not selected in the manner 
in which regular employees are selected. In other words the requirements for selection are not as 
rigorous. There are also other provisions relating to regular service such as the liability of a member of 
the service to be transferred, and his being subject to the disciplinary jurisdiction of the authorities as 
prescribed, which the daily-rated workmen are not subjected to. They cannot, therefore, be equated 
with regular workmen for the purposes for their wages. Nor can they claim the minimum of the 
regular pay-scale of the regularly employed” 


Referring to the said legal position the Hon’ble Apex Court in State of Haryana and another vs. Tilak Raj and 
others (2003 (6) SCC 23) held that a scale of pay is attached to a definite post and in case of a daily wager, he 
holds no posts. The I Party neither in her pleadings nor in evidence has made out the particular works she 
performed under the II Party, much less any material is placed by her as to the nature of the duties for which she was 
engaged by the II Party. The contention of the II Party in its Statement of Objection that the engagement of the I 
Party was for meeting the office exigencies to attend some unspecified jobs on payment of daily wage for the work 
performed is thus well founded. 


6. In Mohammed Ashif and others vs. State of Bihar and others (200 (5) SCC 475), the Hon’ble Supreme 
Court held that the question of regularization of services of an Employee may arise only in situations where against 
an available clear vacancy an appointment is made on adhoc or on-daily wage basis by an authority competent to do 
so without any artificial break in service. The second situation in which the regularization could be granted is held 
to be where the initial entry of the employee against an available vacancy was found suffering from some flaws in

the procedure in making the appointment though the person appointing was competent to make such initial 
recruitment and had otherwise followed the procedure prescribed for such recruitment. It is equally held that “the 
all-important condition precedent for such regularization is that the initial entry of such employee must be made 
against the Sanctioned vacancy and by following the Rules and Regulations governing such entry”. 


7. Similarly the constitution bench of the Hon’ble Apex Court in State of Karnataka vs. Uma Devi (2006 (4) 
SCC ) held that “Jf it is a contractual appointment, the appointment comes to an end at the end of the contract, if it 
were an engagement or appointment on daily wages or casual basis, the same would come to an end when it is 
discontinued. Similarly, a temporary employee could not claim to be made permanent on the expiry of his term of 
appointment. It has also to be clarified that merely because a temporary employee or a casual wage worker is 
continued for a time beyond the term of his appointment, he would not be entitled to be absorbed in regular service 
or made permanent, merely on the strength of such continuance, if the original appointment was not made by 
following a due process of selection as envisaged by the relevant rules. It is not open to the court to prevent regular 
recruitment at the instance of temporary employees whose period of employment has come to an end or of ad hoc 
employees who by the very nature of their appointment, do not acquire any right.’ Here in the instant case the I 
party is claiming permanency and seeks for regularization mainly on the so called “long duration of work” 
(emphasis supplied) and not on any other valid ground. The dictum quoted above defeats her claim as it is bereft of 
valid support and devoid of merit. 


8. Most of the rulings placed by the I party are not applicable to the facts of the case on hand. The Verdict of 
the Hon’ble High Court of Madras in V Muthukumarasamy and others vs. The Chairman, LIC, Zonal Office 
dated 2.0.2007 also does not get any application in view of the fact involved in that case as the Petitioners therein 
were sponsored by the Employment Exchange and have been appointed on temporary basis from shortlisted 
candidates. As already observed, the I Party herein was not sponsored by Employment Exchange nor her 
engagement was in a clear vacancy by undergoing the Regular Recruitment process. 


9. The I party further relied upon on the ruling of the Hon’ble High Court of Karnataka, Bengaluru in R V 
Mohan Reddy vs. The Chairman, Karnataka Grameena Bank in WP No. 944/2022 (L-RES) dated 
0.02.2025 awarding 60% of Backwages to the Employee from the date of his termination reckoning the two 
decades of service he had under the management as a Peon on daily wage. As against that, the principle laid down 
by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in a plethora of rulings aforementioned consistently hold that the Casual 
Employment terminates when the same is discontinued, and merely because a temporary or casual worker has been 
engaged beyond the period of his employment, he would not be entitled to be absorbed into regular service or made 
permanent, if the original appointment was not in terms of the process envisaged by the relevant rules. So the legal 
position settled at rest by the Hon’ble Supreme Court disentitles the I party to put forth any claim of reinstatement, 
regularization, continuity of service or back wages with consequential benefits. 


20. To sum up, the solitary materials viz., Ex W-l vouchers show only pay for a single month in the respective 
years and there is no valid material proving that her engagement was continuous in nature and she performed duties 
under the II Party continuously till the date of her disengagement so as to show that her tenure of service at a time 
was more than 240 days in a calendar year and her disengagement was in violation of the provisions of Section 25F 
of the ID Act. So on legal principle and on factual matrix the I Party failed to establish a case on merit justifying the 
relief sought for in the instant Industrial Dispute. Eventually her Claim Petition fails and the same is liable to be 
dismissed. With this view Points No. | to 3 are answered accordingly.

reinstatement and regularization with continuity of Service and other monetory benefits. In order to high light the 
said aspect the II Party has relied upon the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Subedar Singh and others vs. District 
Judge, Mirzapur and another 200 SCC 37. 


5. It is contextually significant to follow the dictum laid down by the Hon’ble Apex Court in State of 
Haryana vs. Jasmer Singh (996 (l) SCC 77) which reads : 


“The respondents, therefore in the present appeals who are employed on daily wages cannot be treated 
as on a par with persons in regular service of the State of Haryana holding similar posts. Daily-rated 
workers are not required to possess the qualifications prescribed for regular workers, nor do they have 
to fulfil the requirement relating to age at the time of recruitment. They are not selected in the manner 
in which regular employees are selected. In other words the requirements for selection are not as 
rigorous. There are also other provisions relating to regular service such as the liability of a member of 
the service to be transferred, and his being subject to the disciplinary jurisdiction of the authorities as 
prescribed, which the daily-rated workmen are not subjected to. They cannot, therefore, be equated 
with regular workmen for the purposes for their wages. Nor can they claim the minimum of the 
regular pay-scale of the regularly employed” 


Referring to the said legal position the Hon’ble Apex Court in State of Haryana and another vs. Tilak Raj and 
others (2003 (6) SCC 23) held that a scale of pay is attached to a definite post and in case of a daily wager, he 
holds no posts. The I Party neither in her pleadings nor in evidence has made out the particular works she 
performed under the II Party, much less any material is placed by her as to the nature of the duties for which she was 
engaged by the II Party. The contention of the II Party in its Statement of Objection that the engagement of the I 
Party was for meeting the office exigencies to attend some unspecified jobs on payment of daily wage for the work 
performed is thus well founded. 


6. In Mohammed Ashif and others vs. State of Bihar and others (200 (5) SCC 475), the Hon’ble Supreme 
Court held that the question of regularization of services of an Employee may arise only in situations where against 
an available clear vacancy an appointment is made on adhoc or on-daily wage basis by an authority competent to do 
so without any artificial break in service. The second situation in which the regularization could be granted is held 
to be where the initial entry of the employee against an available vacancy was found suffering from some flaws in 


5782 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA AUGUST 6, 2025/SHRAVANA 25, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


the procedure in making the appointment though the person appointing was competent to make such initial 
recruitment and had otherwise followed the procedure prescribed for such recruitment. It is equally held that “the 
all-important condition precedent for such regularization is that the initial entry of such employee must be made 
against the Sanctioned vacancy and by following the Rules and Regulations governing such entry”. 


7. Similarly the constitution bench of the Hon’ble Apex Court in State of Karnataka vs. Uma Devi (2006 (4) 
SCC ) held that “Jf it is a contractual appointment, the appointment comes to an end at the end of the contract, if it 
were an engagement or appointment on daily wages or casual basis, the same would come to an end when it is 
discontinued. Similarly, a temporary employee could not claim to be made permanent on the expiry of his term of 
appointment. It has also to be clarified that merely because a temporary employee or a casual wage worker is 
continued for a time beyond the term of his appointment, he would not be entitled to be absorbed in regular service 
or made permanent, merely on the strength of such continuance, if the original appointment was not made by 
following a due process of selection as envisaged by the relevant rules. It is not open to the court to prevent regular 
recruitment at the instance of temporary employees whose period of employment has come to an end or of ad hoc 
employees who by the very nature of their appointment, do not acquire any right.’ Here in the instant case the I 
party is claiming permanency and seeks for regularization mainly on the so called “long duration of work” 
(emphasis supplied) and not on any other valid ground. The dictum quoted above defeats her claim as it is bereft of 
valid support and devoid of merit. 
8. Most of the rulings placed by the I party are not applicable to the facts of the case on hand. The Verdict of 
the Hon’ble High Court of Madras in V Muthukumarasamy and others vs. The Chairman, LIC, Zonal Office 
dated 2.0.2007 also does not get any application in view of the fact involved in that case as the Petitioners therein 
were sponsored by the Employment Exchange and have been appointed on temporary basis from shortlisted 
candidates. As already observed, the I Party herein was not sponsored by Employment Exchange nor her 
engagement was in a clear vacancy by undergoing the Regular Recruitment process. 
9. The I party further relied upon on the ruling of the Hon’ble High Court of Karnataka, Bengaluru in R V 
Mohan Reddy vs. The Chairman, Karnataka Grameena Bank in WP No. 944/2022 (L-RES) dated 
0.02.2025 awarding 60% of Backwages to the Employee from the date of his termination reckoning the two 
decades of service he had under the management as a Peon on daily wage. As against that, the principle laid down 
by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in a plethora of rulings aforementioned consistently hold that the Casual 
Employment terminates when the same is discontinued, and merely because a temporary or casual worker has been 
engaged beyond the period of his employment, he would not be entitled to be absorbed into regular service or made 
permanent, if the original appointment was not in terms of the process envisaged by the relevant rules. So the legal 
position settled at rest by the Hon’ble Supreme Court disentitles the I party to put forth any claim of reinstatement, 
regularization, continuity of service or back wages with consequential benefits. 
20. To sum up, the solitary materials viz., Ex W-l vouchers show only pay for a single month in the respective 
years and there is no valid material proving that her engagement was continuous in nature and she performed duties 
under the II Party continuously till the date of her disengagement so as to show that her tenure of service at a time 
was more than 240 days in a calendar year and her disengagement was in violation of the provisions of Section 25F 
of the ID Act. So on legal principle and on factual matrix the I Party failed to establish a case on merit justifying the 
relief sought for in the instant Industrial Dispute. Eventually her Claim Petition fails and the same is liable to be 
dismissed. With this view Points No. | to 3 are answered accordingly. 
2I. POINT NO. 4: In view of the above discussion, the I party is held as not entitled for any relief.

AWARD 


On failure of conciliation proceeding, the Government of India through the Ministry of Labour, in 
exercise of powers conferred under clause (d) of Sub-section (l) and Sub-section (2A) of Section 0 of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, !947 (4 of 947), vide its Order No. L-260/7/207-IR(M) dated 05.2.207 has been 
pleased to refer the following dispute between the employer, that is the Management of SAIL-ISP, Burnpur and 
their workman for adjudication by this Tribunal. 


5796 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA AUGUST 6, 2025/SHRAVANA 25, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


“Whether the action of the management of M/s. SAIL-ISP, Burnpur, in not paying the applicable House 
Rent Allowance to Sri Dinesh Sharma from September 203 even though the workman vacated his quarters is just 
and legal? If not, to what relief the workman is entitled to?” 


l. On receiving Order No. L-260/7/207-IR(M) dated 05.2.20l7 from the Government of India, 
Ministry of Labour, New Delhi for adjudication of the dispute, a Reference case No. 2 of 207 was registered on 
9.2.207 and an order was passed for issuing notice to the parties through registered post, directing them to 
appear and submit their written statements along with relevant documents in support of their claims. 


2. Dinesh Sharma filed written statement in this case on 2.02.20l8. Fact of the case as disclosed in the 
written statement is that Dinesh Sharma, bearing P.No. 66577 is a permanent employee of SAIL-ISP, Burnpur and 
is posted as Sr. Technician Traffic at SAIL-ISP, Burnpur. He submitted an application before the management of 
the company on !2.08.20I3 for surrendering his quarters bearing No. KS-23/3&4. The two single units of quarters 
were surrendered by him on 04.09.203. The contention of the workman is that though he has surrendered and 
delivered possession of the quarters on 04.09.203, the management has not paid him any House Rent Allowance 
since September 20l3 after several representation in this matter. Mr. Anupam Roy, DGM (TS), SAIL-ISP, 
Burnpur in his correspondence with ALC (C), Asansol on 08.05.20l7 admitted that the quarters were taken over 
by Town service Department on 04.09.20l3 but as per internal guidelines dated 9.08.203, House Rent 
Allowance could not be granted to Dinesh Sharma. The management however failed to produce any such 
guidelines dated 9.08.203 disqualifying Dinesh Sharma from his right to shelter. Workman further contended 
that management cannot deny him payment of House Rent Allowance under any circumstances. In this Industrial 
Dispute raised by the union on behalf of the workman, it is contended that the workman is entitled to get House 
Rent Allowance from the employer on account of his employment from September 203. 


3. The management of the employer company contested the Industrial Dispute by filing written statement on 
30.05.208 through Mr. Anupam Roy, DGM (TS), SAIL-ISP, Burnpur. It is contended therein that the Industrial 
Dispute is not maintainable under the law. It is admitted that Dinesh Sharma along with two others have 
surrendered their quarters and submitted applications for payment of House Rent Allowance as per prescribed rules 
of the company. The management claimed to have enquired and investigated into the matter and also heard the 
concerned workman. It was found that the name of Dinesh Sharma was not recorded in the Receiving Register and 
there was no entry in the Receiving Register that application had been filed on surrendering of quarters. It is 
further contended that the workman is not entitled to any House Rent Allowance as prayed for and the Industrial 
Dispute raised by him is liable to be dismissed. 


4. To establish his claim Dinesh Sharma has been examined as WW-|. He has reiterated the case disclosed 
in the written statement and filed a copy of his application regarding surrender of his quarters bearing no. No. KS- 
23/3&4, Burnpur. The copy of application appears to have been received by the representative of the company on 
2.08.203. The copy of application is admitted in evidence as Exhibit W-l. The workman stated that he has 
surrendered the quarters on 04.09.203. In his evidence, the witness produced the following documents: 


(i) Copy of application of Dinesh Sharma dated 2.08.203 as Exhibit ४४-।. 


(ii) Letter dated 02.09.20I3 issued by K.N. Bhattacharjee, Assistant Manager (Estate) addressed to 
Sk. F.A. Siddique has been produced as Exhibit W-2. 


(iii) A document relating to handing over possession of the quarters by Dinesh Sharma in good 
condition bearing signatures of Dinesh Sharma and Sk. F.A. Siddique, the new allottee has been 
produced as Exhibit W-3. 


(iv) A statement regarding taking over of quarters from Dinesh Sharma and handing over to Sk. F.A. 
Siddique on 04.09.203 has been produced as Exhibit W-3. 


(५) Letter issued by Anupam Roy, DGM (TS) addressed to ALC (Central), Asansol dated 
08.05.20i7 has been produced as Exhibit W-S. In the said letter it is disclosed that as per internal 
guidelines for payment of House Rent Allowance vide Ref. No. PL/OD/I2/l29! dated 
9.08.203, House Rent Allowance may be paid to the employee in the event of non-availability 
of company’s accommodation and the employee cannot surrender his accommodation and claim 
payment of House Rent Allowance. It is further stated in the letter that the application of Dinesh 
Sharma was received after issuance of internal guidelines dated 9.08.203. 


Witness deposed that the application was submitted by the concerned person by hand but no 
receiving stamp was affixed on the application. It is admitted that the quarters has been handed 
over and the Town Service Department has received the same on 04.09.203. 


(vi) Workman has filed a Memo No. LW/Q-L&O Pen/l682 dated 03.06.2004, the document 
indicated that on vacating the Quarter No. KS-23/4 by Sri S.P. Verma on 08.06.2004, the same 
was handed over to Dinesh Sharma. Documents relating to Fitment of items in the said quarters 
have been collectively marked as Exhibit W-6. 


[भाग व--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : अगस्त 6, 2025/श्रावण 25, 947 5797 


(vii) Allotment letter of Quarter No. KS-23/3 in favour of Dinesh Sharma under Memo No. LW/Q- 
L&O Pen/96l dated 7.05.200 and fitment of items in respect of the quarters have been 
produced as Exhibit W-7. 


In his cross-examination, Dinesh Sharma deposed that he was temporarily allotted with the quarters in the year 
2004 and subsequently in the year 200. Two single units of quarters were allotted in his favour treating them as a 
composite unit. Witness deposed that since he has built his own house, he surrendered company’s quarters in the 
year 20I3 and he is not receiving House Rent Allowance since September 203. Witness denied that the employer 
company has issued any circular notifying that if any quarters is allotted to any employee at any point of time, he 
would not be entitled to House Rent Allowance even after surrendering such quarters. 


5. Management has examined Shri Sanjay Kumar as MW-! who filed his affidavit-in-chief in support of 
management’s case. The witness stated in his affidavit that as per rules, the company does not pay House Rent 
Allowance to employees/workmen in case the housing accommodation is available for such employee. Witness 
further stated that on basis of application/representation of Dinesh Sharma, a committee was constituted by 
management for verification and examining the workman’s claim that he vacated the company’s quarters prior to 
9.08.203. The said committee looked into the records but could not find any documentary evidence to 
substantiate the claim of the workman that he had submitted the application for vacating company’s quarters on 
2.08.203. As such his claim was denied. In his Examination-in-chief, the management witness stated that 
employee is entitled to 20% of basic pay as House Rent Allowance but if he has any quarters under his possession 
or occupation, he will not be entitled to House Rent Allowance. In course of his cross-examination, the witness 
admitted that Dinesh Sharma has surrendered his quarters on 04.09.20I3 and the possession of same was taken 
over by the Civil and Electrical department of the company. Management has produced some documents relating 
to payment of House Rent Allowance to the employees of SAIL and internal guidelines dated 9.08.203 which 
have been collectively marked as Exhibit M-Series. It transpires from his evidence that though in the paragraph 
three (3) of his affidavit he stated that as per rules of the company, no House Rent Allowance is granted to the 
employees in case housing accommodation is available for such employees, he has not produced the rules in 
support thereof. 


6. The crux of the issue in this case is whether Dinesh Sharma, who surrendered company’s accommodation 
on 04.09.203 is entitled to any House Rent Allowance or not? 


7. Mr. Ayan Ranjan Mukherjee, learned advocate for the management of SAIL-ISP arguing the case 
submitted that there is no dispute regarding handing over possession of allotted quarters by the Dinesh Sharma on 
04.09.20i3. He also concedes the facts that a person not enjoying any accommodation of the company is entitled to 
House Rent Allowance but for the purpose of claiming the same he has to submit his application in a prescribed 
format superscribed as ‘Format for application for grant_of House Rent Allowance’. Alternatively, learned 
advocate argued that the issue of House Rent Allowance for new recruits has been covered by internal guidelines 
where it is decided that in interest of uniformity, both executive and non-executive employees who want House 
Rent Allowance may apply for payment of House Rent Allowance as per the standard format. It is further asserted 
that the internal guidelines provide the employees who are availing House Rent Allowance facility may be 
persuaded to shift to quarters and the Estate Department may write to the concerned employees advising them to 
apply for quarters. In the event quarters are allotted, House Rent Allowance facilities would be withdrawn. 
Learned advocate argued that since the aggrieved workman did not submit his application in standard format, he is 
not entitled to receive House Rent Allowance. 


8. Mr. P.K. Das, learned advocate for the union argued that there is no internal guideline of the employer 
company disqualifying the workman from receiving House Rent Allowance even when he has surrendered his 
quarters. It is argued that the workman has surrendered his quarters on 04.09.203. As such he is entitled to House 
Rent Allowance from September 203 till date. 


9. I have considered the arguments advanced by learned advocates for the management and union 
representing the aggrieved workman. Also considered the pleading of parties and evidence adduced by them in 
support of their case. Admittedly the workman who was allotted two units of quarters at different timesfor his 
accommodation bearing No. KS-23/3 and No. KS-23/4, surrendered the quarters to Assistant Manager (Estate), 
SAIL-HSCO Steel Plant, Burnpur and his application was received by the office on 2.08.203 (Exhibit ४४-।). The 
said quarters was allotted to Sk. F.A. Siddiqui on 04.09.203 and the same finds support from document filed as 
Exhibit W-2, W-3 and W-4. The workman has claimed for House Rent Allowance from September 20!3 which 
has been denied by the management. Hence, this dispute. It is gathered from Exhibit M-Series that an internal 
guideline dated 9.08.20I3 has been issued by Sr. Manager (Personnel-OD) of SAIL-ISP, Burnpur bearing 
No. PL/OD/2/29], which states that in case of new employees in the company, in the event of non-availability of 
accommodation, House Rent Allowance may be paid and the concerned employee on submitting application in 
standard format to the concerned establishment section of the Personnel Department. It is clear that this provision 
is applicable only in the case of new employees. 


5798 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA AUGUST 6, 2025/SHRAVANA 25, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


0. In the latter portion of the guideline it is provided that considering the present condition of K/KA type 
quarters, the new ACTs/OCTs who do not accept the said quarters may be paid House Rent Allowance after 
completion of their training period and placement in the regular grade subject to the condition that better type 
quarters are not available for allotment to the concerned employee, and the Estate Department certifies to this 
effect. The said provision is not applicable to Dinesh Sharma since he is not a new employee. In as much as the 
employees who are already availing HRA facility, the Estate Department has been advised to write letters to the 
concerned employees advising them to apply for quarters and in event of allotment of the same the HRA facility 
would be withdrawn. In the instant case, the workman has surrendered his KS type quarters. Management has not 
been able to produce any document to indicate that the Estate Department had communicated such provision of 
internal guideline to the workman or offered any better quarters to him. The workman is still in the service of the 
company and raised the dispute in the year 20l7. According to the guidelines of the company, employees 
surrendering their quarters within a period of one year prior to the scheduled date of superannuation 


will not be entitled to receive House Rent Allowance. The corollary deduced from this is that a person who 
surrendered his quarters long before his superannuation or more than one year before his superannuation is entitled 
to House Rent Allowance. Under the facts and circumstances, I hold that the aggrieved workman Dinesh Sharma is 
entitled to receive House Rent Allowance from 04.09.203 till date according to the prevailing rates applicable. 
For the purpose of receiving House Rent Allowance, the workman is required to submit his application in the 
standard format which has to be provided to him by the Estate Department. 


Hence, 
ORDERED 


The Industrial Dispute is allowed on contest in favour of the workman. Management of SAIL-ISP, 
Burnpur is directed to pay House Rent Allowance to Dinesh Sharma w.e.f. 04.09.203 till date, on the basis of 
applicable rates from time to time. The management shall pay current and arrear House Rent Allowance to the 
concerned workman within two months from the date of communication of order on receiving his application in 
standard/prescribed format which shall be submitted within a fortnight from the Award. Let an Award be drawn up 
on the basis of my above findings. Let copies of the Award in duplicate be sent to the Ministry of Labour, 
Government of India, New Delhi for information and Notification.

As per letter dated 07//204 by the Government of India, Ministry of Labour, New Delhi, the reference 
has been made to this Tribunal under Section-!0 of Industrial Disputes Act, 947 (in short the ‘Act’)as per 
Notification No. L-2202/62/20l4(IR(CM-ID) dt. 07//204. The dispute under reference relates to: 


584 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA AUGUST 6, 2025/SHRAVANA 25, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


“HAMS Ho सी० एम० सोहागपुर क्षेत्र एसईसीएल प्रबंधन TART श्री शेख AYA, एक्स वरि० मिस्त्री को 
प्राथमिक रिकार्ड में दर्ज जन्मलिथी को अनदेखा कर पश्चातवर्ती बनाये गये सेवाअशिनेयखों में दर्ज (Heol जन्मतिथी 
के आधार पर समय पूर्व सेवानिवृत कर दिया जाना क्या न्यायसंगत & यदि नहीं; तो कर्मकार FA अनुतोष पाने का 
हकदार हैं?” 


Case of the workman, is mainly that he was appointed with the Management on the post of Motor 
Mechanic on 0.02.975, his date of birth was wrongly mentioned by Management in their records as 0.07.952 
whereas it was 0.0.953 as show in her mark sheet of Class 5" and State Board of Education. He was issued a 
letter of superannuation by Management on the basis of wrong date of birth recorded by Management in their 
records. He filed a writ petition No. |754/200 before Hon’ble High Court of M.P. at Jabalpur which was heard and 
disposed vide order dated 24.02.200 with a direction to Management to place his case before the Age 
Determination Committee for determination of his date of birth and age. This order was not compiled by the 
Management hence, the Workman was forced to file a Contempt petition No. 703/200. During the pendency of the 
contempt petition, Management decided its representation vide its order dated 0.05.200 rejecting his claim and 
holding his date of birth recorded in their records as correct. He filed another Writ Petition No. 9004/20I] against 
this order of Management dated !0.05.20I0 rejecting his representation. In the last pay certificate issued to him by 
Management on his transfer from Dhanpuri to Amlai, the date of birth of the applicant, the date of appointment and 
the PF No. were incorrectly recorded. After the Workman pointed out this error before Management at Amlai, they 
sent a communication to Dhanpuri from where the Workman was transferred to Amlai confirming the date of birth 
and date of appointment as well PF No. of the Workman but they did not response to this letter and the Management 
passed the order dated !0.05.200 ignoring his date of birth recorded in his Higher Secondary Certificate. The said 
writ petition was disposed by Hon’ble High Court vide its order dated 28.06.20l2 directing the Management to 
conduct a fresh inquiry with respect to determination of age of the Workman taking into account the original 
documents or relevant documents produced at the time of initial appointment of the Workman. It was further 
directed that, if it is found that the date of birth was incorrectly recorded in the service rules, the same would be 
corrected and the Workman would be superannuated according to the correct date of birth of the Workman. It was 
also directed that this exercise will be completed within I5 days and till the order is communicated to the petitioner 
by Management, the petitioner Workman shall be allowed to continue in employment. It is further the case of the 
Workman that Management did not comply this order of Hon’ble High Court and communicated to the Workman 
vide their letter dated 23.08.202 that he is superannuated w.e.f. 30.06.202 which is unjust, illegal and arbitrary 
because it is against the provisions in this respect. The Workman has prayed that, holding the action of Management 
in superannuating the Workman on the basis of his date of birth 0.07.952 against law, he be held entitled to be 
reinstated with back wages and benefits in service and post retrial benefits. 


Case of Management is mainly that, the Workman was initially appointed w.e.f. 0.04.976 at the time of 
his initial appointment he declared his age as 28 years as on !980, which was recorded in the Form B register and 
they are connected registers/ documents which was never challenged by the Workman. The entries were recorded in 
it has been certified by the Workman himself. Now at the fag end, he has challenged his date of birth and 
superannuation which is not permissible in law. Management has prayed that, their action is not false in law and the 
reference may be answered against the Workman. 


In evidence, the Workman has filed his affidavit as his examination-in-chief. He has been cross-examined 
on his affidavit by Management. He has further filed and proved photocopy documents, his last pay certificate, letter 
of Management dated 0.05.200 rejecting his representation, copy of order of Hon’ble High Court in the W.P. No. 
9004/20I, letter of Management dated 23.08.202 sent by Deputy General Manager Sohagpur Area to Deputy 
General Manager Amlai, Superannuation order, order of Hon’ble High Court in Contempt Petition No. 558/202, 
his original Identity Card, duplicate copy of his Secondary School Marksheet, and Technical Education Mark sheet 
which have been proved as Exhibit W- to W-0 to be referred as and when required. 


Management has filed affidavit of its witness as his examination-in-chief which has been cross-examined 
by the Workman side. Management has further filed and proved photocopy Form B (Exhibit ॥/| & M/2), Last Pay 
Certificate (Exhibit M/3), Copy of Service Books of the Workman (Exhibit M-4) and Copy of Form PS-3 and PS-4 
filed as (Exhibit — M/5 & M/6). 


I have heard argument of Learned Counsel for Workman Mr. Shakil Ahmed and for Management Mr. 
Neeraj Kewat. I have gone through the record as well. 


The undisputed facts are mainly that, the Age Determination Committee determined the age of Workman 
under order of the High Court detailed mentioned earlier, it has been referred by Management in its order dated 
0.05.200 and was confirmed by Management in its order passed by it in-compliance of order of Hon’ble High 
Court dated 28.06.20I2 passed in W.P. No. 9004/20! retreating the previous decision taken by the Age 
Determination Committee. The issue which arises therefore is as follows: 


[भाग वा--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : अगस्त 6, 2025/श्रावण 25, 947 585 


Whether the decision of Management passed by the Report of Age Determination Committee in holding 
the date of birth of the Workman as 07.707953 is correct in law. 


The Implementation Instructions-37(I.I.37) prepared in the light of NCWA-II provides procedure for 
determination/verification of age of its employees. A(i & ii) of the LI.-37 is relevant in this respect and it is being 
reproduced as follows: 


A) Determination of the age at the time of first appointment: 


i) Matriculates : In the case of Appointees, who have been passed Matriculation or Qualification 
Examination, the date of birth recorded in the said certificate shall be treated as correct date of 
birth and the same will not be altered in any circumstances. 


ii) Non-Matriculates but educated : In the case of appointees who have pursued studies in a 
recognized educational institution, the date of birth recorded in the School Leaving Certificate 
shall be treated as correct date of birth and the same will not be altered at any circumstances. 


It is the case of the Workman that, he did file the duplicate certificate of his Secondary School 
Examination which he passed in 97 and is conducted by Education Board. His date of birth was recorded as 
0I.0.953. The report of the Age Determination Committee,which is the basis of the order dated l0.05.200 has 
also been filed by the Management, which is Exhibit M-7. Perusal of this report goes to show that Workman did file 
duplicate copy of Pramanpatra of Sambhagiya Purv Madhyamik Pareeksha,l97! and duplicate copy of Provisional 
Central Vocational Certificate of 973 in which his date of birth was recorded as 0.0.953. He also filed his 
Identity card issued by Western Division of Coal Mines Authority Sohagpur Area, indicating his date of birth as 
0I.0.953. His last pay certificate issued by Dhanpuri Area indicates his date of birth as 28 years as on 980. The 
age determination committee relied upon the Form-B register of Amlai area, Service Register of the Workman, 
Form PS 3 and 4, Form B Register of Dhanpuri Area where his date of birth has been indicated as 28 years on 980. 
The age determination committee records further that, there is no prove that the State Educational Certificate in the 
Trade of Motor Mechanic indicating his date of birth of the Workman as 0.0.953 was filed by the Workman at 
the time of his appointment, also that the Identity Card issued by Sohagpur Area indicating his date of Birth as 
0I.0.953 could be manipulated and hence held the claim of the workman not proved and since his date of birth is 
recorded as 0I.07.952 in Registers of Management and also the Workman refused to undergo radiological test 
therefore his date of Birth is 0!.0.l953 cannot be accepted. Based on the finding of this Report of Age 
Determination Committee, the order of Management dated 0.05.20l0 was passed and the second order in 
compliance of the second Writ W.P. No. 2004/202 simply retreats the previous order. 


It is not disputed that the Workman was first appointed as Motor Mechanic on 0.02.975 or even if the 
case of the Management be taken in this respect, then on 0.04.976. 


The minimum required qualification for the Post of Motor Mechanic is that the Applicant must be 
having Vocational Certificate recognized by any institutions, with respect to Motor Mechanic Trade. Without this 
the Workman cannot be appointed as Motor Mechanic. 


Naturally, he would have been selected for appointment as a Motor Mechanic after the Management 
satisfied with him that he has cleared the Vocational Certificate with respect to the trade. The Vocational Certificate 
of the Workman filed on record proved and shows that he cleared this examination in 973 that is before he was 
appointed by Management. The Sambhagiya Purv Madhyamik Pareeksha was also cleared by him in 97] i.e. 
before his appointment in 975/976. 


Case of the Management with respect to grounds for rejecting the representation of the Workman on the 
basis of report of Age Determination Committee is that According to Age Determination Committee, there was no 
proof that these documents were submitted by the Workman at the time of his appointment. Since, the post on which 
the Workman was first appointed required certain Vocational Qualifications for appointment which the Workman 
possessed undisputedly, it cannot be imagined that he did not produce any Certificate with respect to his Vocational 
Qualification i.e. the first requirement for his selection to the post. In the light of this discussion, it can be held that 
the Age Determination Committee committed error in law in not relying on provision in I.I.-37 with respect to 
determining the age of the Workman by not placing reliance on his Vocational and Purva Madhyamik Academic 
Certificates which were to be first relied upon. Consequently, the action of Management, in rejecting the 
Representation of the Workman on the basis of report of Age Determination Committee and Superannuating the 
Workman on the basis of his date of birth recorded as 0.07.952 in his service records mainly by Management is 
held unjust, illegal and arbitrary. 


Issue is answered accordingly. 


586 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA AUGUST 6, 2025/SHRAVANA 25, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


On the basis of above discussion, the reference is answered as follows. 
AWARD 


Holding the action of Management of Amlai OCM Sohagpur Area, SECL in superannuating the 
Workman Sheikh Kayyum, Senior Mechanic on the basis of his date of birth dated 0.07.952 as illegal, 
unjust and arbitrary, the Workman is held entitled to be deemed in service till the date of superannuation 
based on his date of birth 0.0.953 with all back-wages and pre as well post-retrial benefits. 


The Workman is also held entitled to litigation cost Rs. 25,000/- from Management in view of the 
checkered litigation in the case in hand. 


Management is directed to settle the entire dues of the Workman within 60 days from the date of 
publication of Award in the Gazette, failing which interest @8 per annum from the date of publication of 
Award till payment.

As per letter dated [4/07/20 by the Government of India, Ministry of Labour, New Delhi, the reference 
has been made to this Tribunal under Section-l0 of Industrial Disputes Act, !947 (in short the ‘Act’) as per 
Notification No. L-2202/85/20(IR(CM-ID) dt. 4/07/20l. The dispute under reference relates to: 


“Whether the action of the management of the Sohagpur Area of SECL not making necessary 
corrections in the Date of Birth of Shri Keshavram S/o Shyamlal in his service records and forcibly 
retiring him on the basis of wrong entry of date of birth is legal and justified? To what relief the 
claimant is entitled for and from which date?” 


Notices were issued to the parties. They appeared and filed their respective statement of claim and 
defense. 


Case of the Workman is mainly that, he was appointed on 29.06.990 as a loader on compassionate 
ground, he had produced proof of his age at the time of his initial appointment which was his Middle Class 
Certificate containing his date of birth as 0.0.957. The Management arbitrarily recorded his date of birth as 32 
years in !98! meaning thereby his age at the time of appointment to be treated as 4| years and ] months. 


On coming to know about this anomaly, he made representation before Management and requested to 
correct his date of birth. The Management rejected the representation vide its order dated 0.06.990. He then 
preferred a Writ Petition No. 4585/2007 which was disposed by Hon’ble High Court of M.P. at Jabalpur with a 
direction to avail the remedy in Industrial Law. 


According to the Workman, he was superannuated on the basis of his wrong date of birth which is 
unjust, illegal and arbitrary. He raised a dispute before Assistant Labour Commissioner which could not be 
conciliated hence this reference. The Workman has prayed that holding his superannuation on the basis of his 
wrong date of birth recorded by Management in its documents, against law, he be held entitled to be reinstated and 
to be superannuated on the date fixed according to his correct date of birth as mentioned in his School Certificate. 


Case of the Management is mainly that, the Workman was appointed on the compassionate basis after 
his father was declared medically unfit on 29.06.l990. He had declared himself illiterate at the time of his 
appointment. His date of birth was recorded as 0.07.949 on the statutory records maintained by Management. 
On his disclosure, his date of birth was recorded in Form B and other registers like Service Registers, PS 4, PS 3 
etc. He made a representation before Management seeking correction of his date of birth on the basis of School 
leaving Certificate. It was found that, there was no justification of filing the School Leaving Certificate with such a 
delay. He could not substantiate his claim, hence his representation was dismissed. He was superannuated on the 
basis of his date of birth recorded in his Service Record. Management has requested that the reference be answered 
against the Management. 


The Workman has filed his rejoinder in which he has mainly retreated his claim. 


In evidence, the Workman has filed and proved his photocopy school certificate, order of Management 
dated 0.06.2009 rejecting his representation, he also filed his affidavit as his examination in chief. He has been 
cross-examined by the Management. 


Management filed affidavit of its witness as his examination in chief. He has been cross-examined by 
Workman side. The Management has filed and proved Exhibit ४-। the Application of the Workman, M-2 School 
Leaving Certificate, M-3 another Application of the Workman, Copy of Form B Register, and Service Book. 


None appeared for Workman at the stage of argument. I have heard argument of Learned Counsel 
Mr. Neeraj Kewat for Management. I have gone through the record as well. 


588 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA AUGUST 6, 2025/SHRAVANA 25, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


No written arguments have been filed by any of the parties. 
On perusal of record in the light of rival arguments following issued arises for determination 


Whether the Management has committed correctly in law in rejecting the representation of the Workman 
with respect to the correction of his date of birth? 


The Implementation Instructions 76 prepared under National Coal Wage Agreement- II which deal with 
the disputes regarding age/ date of birth of the Workman requires to be referred here and which is being referred as 
follows. 

B) Determination of the age at the time of first appointment: 


iii) Matriculates : In the case of Appointees, who have been passed Matriculation or Qualification 
Examination, the date of birth recorded in the said certificate shall be treated as correct date 
of birth and the same will not be altered in any circumstances. 


iv) Non-Matriculates but educated : In the case of appointees who have pursued studies in a 
recognized educational institution, the date of birth recorded in the School Leaving Certificate 
shall be treated as correct date of birth and the same will not be altered at any circumstances. 


v) Ex-Servicemen: 


In the case of Ex-servicemen who are not matricula-tes, the date of birth recorded in the Army 
Discharge Certificate shall be treated as correct date of birth and the same will not be altered 
under any circumstances. 


vi) Illiterates : 


In the case of appointees not covered by the fore-going clauses, the date of birth will be 
determined by the Colliery Medical Officer keeping in view any documentary or other relevant 
evidence as may be produced by the appointee. Date of birth so deter-mined shall be treated as 
correct date of birth and the same will not be altered under any circumstances 


The order of the Management rejecting representation of the Workman, which is 09 record, goes to 
show that the Duplicate Marksheet of School Examination, [970 does not contain the date of its issuing. The 
Workman could not explain inordinate delay in seeking correction of his date of birth. And his representation was 
dismissed. 


It was incumbent on the Workman to proof the date of birth as recorded in is School Certificate which is 
un-dated. By way of producing the Register Form where the Certificate was issued and also examining the 
Headmaster or Concern person who had issue the copy in absence of this evidences, the Management could not be 
said to have acted against law in not relying on the undated certificate. I do not find any illegality in this action of 
Management. 


Accordingly, holding the action of Management in not correcting the date of birth of the Workman and 
superannuating him on the basis of his date of birth recorded in his service documents just and proper, the issue 
stands answered accordingly. 


On the basis of above discussion and findings the reference is answered as follows. 
AWARD 


Holding the Management in not correcting the date of birth of the Workman and superannuating 
him on the basis of his date of birth recorded in his service documents is just and proper. He is entitled to no 
relief. 


No order as to cost.
